title: The Mind of Mattathias: Let's Search the Scriptures

sense.text:
“For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning,” Mattathias drew on what had already been written. His mind was formed by Israel's history, and that history gave him the understanding to encourage his sons and begin an uprising when the people were oppressed. The feast of dedication recalls overcoming the oppressor, so its history should form a warrior's mind rather than a victim's mind.

Paul wrote while Rome held power and could examine the letters of the Jews. His writing could not always be as open as he wished, but the scriptures still reveal a soldier's understanding. Read the history with the purpose of learning how to remain faithful and do the work in the conditions now before us.

“Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.” A soldier's mind is on the battle. In Paul's time the fight being described was not a physical uprising, and the present work is spiritual warfare. Enduring hardness means becoming serious about strengthening the troop, building brothers and preparing them to do the work throughout the twelve tribes worldwide. Travel for the work is not a vacation: study with the men, build them up, go into the streets with them and show them how to contend in the spirit.

Hardness includes personal trials at work and in daily life, marital trials, and trials within the congregation. The marital trial also includes the unmarried man or woman waiting faithfully instead of burning in lust and abandoning discipline. Congregational trials likewise have to be endured. The soldier's responsibility is to overcome personal faults, keep the commandments and push the truth rather than allow those pressures to turn him aside.

precepts.why:
“The Lord is a man of war:” The soldier's mind agrees with the mind of God. When Israel kept the commandments, the Lord enabled the people to overcome their enemies. When Israel fell away, he used those enemies to make war against Israel and bring the people into slavery. His being a man of war does not mean he protects disobedience from its consequences.

Chattel slavery and the later systems of oppression, including Reconstruction, Black Codes, Jim Crow and the struggle continuing through the civil-rights era, are set in that history of forsaking the commandments. Returning requires obedience, spiritual discipline and the willingness to do the work. The Lord has an army, and Israel's older history shows its order before the time of Paul's letters.

sense.text:
“See, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh:” Moses rose from the condition of his enslaved people to a position of power over Pharaoh. Pharaoh had crossed the Most High, and the man before him now represented divine authority. This is a picture of the power God can place upon his people.

The black man does not find that power in the Christian white nationalist church. Even while being treated as last to be hired and first to be fired, he can sense that his people were made for something greater. Israel is to be gods upon the earth over the nations, though presently living in the vessel of men.

That identity calls for a warrior's mind instead of a victim's mind. The repeated challenge about remaining fat and obese is a challenge to prepare the body for service and the spiritual battle, rather than become comfortable with inability to go out and work.

The numbering took place in the wilderness of Sinai on the first day of the second month, a new moon, in the second year after coming out of Egypt. These were Israelites who had seen God deliver them through the Red Sea, destroy Pharaoh's army and lead them with the cloud and fire. The congregation was Israel, not the surrounding nations.

Taking the sum means counting the congregation by families and by the houses of their fathers. The same rebuilding now begins with families coming together as a nation. A man whose father is an Israelite is an Israelite; descent is reckoned through the father's house. The count was of the males by their polls.

“From twenty years old and upward, all that are able to go forth to war in Israel:” Twenty is used as the age of a man in this service. Younger men receive some allowance, but there is still a responsibility to train and care for the body rather than normalize young men being obese.

Moses and Aaron numbered Israel by armies. There were armies within the greater army of Israel, with leaders and order in the tribes. Elders, bishops and deacons in the New Testament carry that principle of order under different words; Israel did not have to learn the idea of an organized body from Rome.

Each man pitched by his own standard and the ensign of his father's house. The twelve-tribe flags recall those standards; Judah's lion is one example. The flags and ordered formation are drawn from scripture, not invented without a foundation.

The camp of Judah was numbered at 186,400 throughout its armies and set forth first. Reuben's standard was on the south, also according to its armies. Israel possessed military structure long before the Roman army and even before the Babylonian army. The claim that this order was borrowed from Esau reverses the history.

The present formations are a rehearsal in the spirit of unity, discipline and readiness. They need to improve, including the men's physical readiness. Reuben's place also rebukes the idea that the northern kingdom is inherently weak; that history belongs to the whole nation.

Reuben's camp was numbered throughout its armies and moved in the second rank. Do not skip over the repeated reference to armies. Israel was one nation with ordered companies within it, moving according to a common structure.

Ephraim's camp numbered 108,100 and moved in the third rank. Puerto Rican brothers are reminded that they have a history of mighty men in the scriptures. That history should raise their understanding of themselves and move them toward the work. Remaining in the red or yellow fitness categories sixteen months after the men's conference is challenged as a refusal to prepare, not a condition to become content with.

The first, second and third ranks show order and instruction. God does not need every unwilling man, as Gideon's history will demonstrate, but each man should take responsibility to become fit for the battle.

precepts.why:
The places of drawing water are the places of servitude and captivity where Israel was scattered. There “shall they rehearse the righteous acts of the Lord,” Rehearsal includes keeping the commandments, going out to teach them and learning to move together in one mind and one spirit.

The noise of archers is understood as more than a man shooting an old wooden bow. The focus is deliverance in the places of oppression and preparation there. Present marching and organized outreach are rehearsals of unity; the ordered armies in Numbers supply the historical foundation.

sense.text: The fearful were permitted to depart from mount Gilead. Twenty-two thousand returned, leaving ten thousand. God does not require a vast number of men to deliver his people. Reluctance, excuses and failure to prepare the body for the work are challenged as fear: professing readiness while seldom going to camp does not demonstrate a warrior's mind.

“The people are yet too many;” God brought the remaining men to a test at the water and determined who would go. The selection distinguished men who could act selflessly for the mission from those focused on themselves. Likewise, requirements placed before the body try whether men will actually do what they have agreed to do, rather than repeat the same promise many months later.

The distinction at the water showed awareness. The three hundred brought water to their mouths with their hands and could keep looking around at the whole situation. The other 9,700 are presented as absorbed in satisfying themselves rather than watching the wider mission.

God seeks men with vision who consider the whole body. Mattathias had that mind: he considered the circumstances, made decisions and drew people through strength and leadership. He would not have belonged with the 9,700. The blunt warning to men who remain unwilling is that God does not need them; the provocation is to stop choosing weakness and selfishness and become ready to serve.

Israel again did evil, and the Lord strengthened Eglon king of Moab against the nation. This is the recurring pattern of sin, captivity and deliverance. Eglon gathered Ammon and Amalek, struck Israel and possessed the city of palm trees. Smiting Israel was a national conquest, not merely striking one person. Israel served him eighteen years.

The city of palm trees recalls the land from which the people came, in contrast with many of the cold cities in which they now live. The oppression was real and extended through almost twenty years.

When the people cried to the Lord, he raised Ehud as a deliverer, just as he had raised Moses in response to Israel's oppression in Egypt. Ehud was a left-handed Benjamite. That history calls Benjamin to strength and preparation rather than accepting a condition unfit for the work.

Ehud made and concealed a double-edged dagger and brought a present to Eglon. His approach showed forethought, tact and a plan, not an aimless reaction. Eglon is described as a very fat man, living in power while Israel served him. The comparison with men neglecting their own fitness is meant to provoke them away from resembling the oppressor rather than the deliverer.

This was the act of the deliverer God raised at that historical time. It is not an instruction to make a dagger and attack a ruler today. The present charge is spiritual warfare and service to the people.

Ehud gained a private audience with the king and the confidence needed for the attendants to withdraw. That shows the importance of strategy and understanding a situation. Eglon trusted the man who had come with a present, then heard that he had a message from God. Ehud's left-handed action and the concealed weapon completed the purpose for which he had entered. The length of the dagger is connected to Eglon's great size.

The account demonstrates the skill of a tactician who could enter, carry out the task and leave, rather than a man merely boasting about courage. His purpose was the deliverance of Israel from the king's oppression.

Ehud escaped while the others delayed, passed the quarries and reached Seirath. The quarries are explained as worked-out pits, like places that later fill with water. He then blew a trumpet in mount Ephraim, and Israel came down after him. The signal and response show a plan shared beforehand.

“and he before them.” He went ahead of the people. Leadership means setting the example and going into the work, not asking others to move while remaining behind. His readiness enabled him to complete one task and immediately lead the next.

Ehud called Israel to follow because the Lord had delivered Moab into their hands. The men secured the passages of Jordan and defeated about ten thousand men of valour without allowing them to escape. Moab was subdued under Israel. The Lord had answered Israel's cry through a deliverer who acted and led.

That history is used to challenge men who cannot even make themselves available for camp. Wanting the appearance or name of a mighty man while avoiding the work does not match the forefathers' example.

Shamgar son of Anath slew six hundred Philistines with an ox goad and delivered Israel. The goad is a spiked stick used to drive cattle. The action is attributed to Shamgar himself, showing the power of the Lord upon the man rather than dependence on a great troop or modern weapons.

Israel has a history of righteous war in which God raised men to deliver the nation. The present work likewise requires men raised in the spirit to serve. Taking the name of a mighty forefather should bring a corresponding desire to become useful and prepared, not merely a name without the mind behind it.

Israel had prepared for war by securing the hill-country passages, fortifying the high places and laying impediments. The high ground gave a defensive advantage, and the impediments obstructed the approaches. The enemy later used a different method, cutting the water supply and wearing the people down through attrition rather than relying only on an uphill assault.

Holofernes called the princes of Moab, captains of Ammon and governors of the sea coast to consider Israel's power, army and king. Even the heathen understood the need for counsel and strategy. Their discussion recognized Israel as a people with a history and a power that could not safely be ignored.

The account before the enemy recalled Israel crying to God, the incurable plagues in Egypt, the drying of the Red Sea and the journey through Sinai and Cades-Barne. It continued through the defeat of the people of Heshbon, the crossing of Jordan and the removal of the Canaanites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Sychemites and Gergesites. The surrounding nations knew how God had made room for Israel and given the people victory.

The enemy looked for error and sin among Israel because that would be their ruin. They understood that when Israel was right with God, he fought for the nation. The present low condition of the people is likewise connected to departing from God's commandments. Upholding a white Christ and teaching that belief removes the need for obedience leaves the people without the understanding of how their strength was lost.

The later siege brought hunger and thirst severe enough that some proposed surrender. This prepares the setting for Judith's response: faith and remembrance of the forefathers rather than assuming that oppression had made deliverance impossible.

Judith's husband Manasses was of her own tribe and kindred and died in the barley harvest while overseeing the work in the fields. He had responsibility, workers and resources. The household he left and Judith's understanding show a woman who had been well established and taught. Judith is identified with the tribe of Simeon through her family history.

She fasted throughout her widowhood except for the eves of the Sabbaths, the Sabbaths, the eves of the new moons, the new moons and the feast and solemn days of Israel. This shows discipline joined to honouring the holy days. Her continued honour for her husband is presented as part of the character that made her trustworthy.

Judith challenged the decision that effectively put a deadline on God. “who are ye that have tempted God this day,” She feared tempting him. Such fortitude came through being raised in the fear of God and understanding his commandments. It contradicts the idea that God's people could dispense with keeping them.

“he hath power to defend us when he will, even every day, or to destroy us before our enemies.” The elders had spoken of waiting five days. God's power was not confined to their timetable. The faithful response was to wait upon him rather than make surrender the inevitable conclusion if he did not act on command.

The brethren depended upon their leaders' example, and the sanctuary, house and altar rested upon them. Judith urged thanksgiving in the trial and remembrance of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob's experience while keeping Laban's sheep in Mesopotamia. She drew strength from the same history Mattathias would later use with his sons.

The nation had been taught to fear God and remember how the fathers overcame. Even its enemies knew that history. The degraded descriptions now placed upon our people do not define what Israel is. The history supplies a greater identity and a reason to remain faithful under pressure.

Judith proposed an act that would be remembered through the generations. She would go out with her waitingwoman, her handmaid, while the men stood at the gate, and trusted that God would visit Israel through her hand. She withheld the details until the act was finished.

Her plan used her beauty, discipline and understanding of people to help the men and deliver the nation. As with Ehud, gaining access depended on more than physical force. If she had bluntly announced that she would cut that nigga's head off, the men seeking to protect her would not have wanted her to go. Instead she asked them to trust her, supported by her character and reputation.

She spoke respectfully to the governors, not as a loud ass woman demanding her own way. Her femininity and restraint were part of the historical example. This is not a command for sisters to carry out such an act today.

“Go in peace, and the Lord God be before thee, to take vengeance on our enemies.” The princes allowed Judith and her maid to leave the defended city even though the hostile army surrounded it. They trusted her and desired deliverance and vengeance against the oppressor. Praying for the overthrow of those oppressing Israel is therefore part of the nation's recorded history. The later songs about Judith remember that deliverance.

The Greeks entered the sanctuary and took the golden altar, candlestick, vessels, shewbread table, veil, crowns, ornaments, silver, gold and hidden treasures. These were sacred to all Israel, but the desecration had particular weight for the Levites, whose life's service was to maintain the things of God's house. Understanding that charge explains why Mattathias, a Levite, was so deeply moved by what he saw.

The plunder was accompanied by a great massacre and proud boasting. The account is not simply the loss of possessions: Israel's people were killed and the holy things entrusted to them were defiled. This forms the background to Mattathias' grief and anger.

Antiochus sent the decree throughout his kingdom that all should become one people and leave their own laws. This imposed unity is compared with the modern ideal of one nation under God and democracy inherited from the Greeks. The heathen agreed, but obedience to that decree required Israel to abandon its own law.

Many Israelites consented to the king's religion, sacrificed to idols and profaned the Sabbath. The king's messengers instructed Jerusalem and the cities of Judah to follow the strange laws of the land. These divisions help explain later estrangement among the tribes and why some Israelites were treated as Greeks or heathen: they had accepted the oppressor's religion and lost the traditions of their fathers. The divisions encountered around the woman at the well and Cornelius are connected to that history.

The books of the law were torn and burned. “the king’s commandment was, that they should put him to death.” Possessing the testament or consenting to the law brought a death sentence under the king's command. The oppression sought to destroy Israel's connection with its scriptures. Mattathias' resistance must be understood against a decree that threatened both life and identity.

Mattathias was the son of John, the son of Simeon, a priest of the sons of Joarib, from Jerusalem and living in Modin. He had five sons: Joannan, Simon, Judas, Eleazar and Jonathan. The strength of his response is connected to a father and grandfather who taught him Israel's history, and to his own raising of sons who shared that understanding.

“wherefore was I born to see this misery of my people,” Mattathias saw the blasphemies, the people in the enemy's hands and the sanctuary given to strangers. The temple had become like a man without glory. His grief concerned the whole nation, with the added weight of a Levite seeing the service entrusted to his tribe desecrated.

“Whosoever is zealous of the law, and maintaineth the covenant, let him follow me.” The call required a choice. Those who would preserve the law and covenant had to stand with it despite the king's decree. Those who stayed under the decree risked losing the law and the traditions of their fathers, becoming indistinguishable from the people whose religion they adopted.

Mattathias and his sons left everything they had in the city and fled to the mountains. This meant leaving established houses and comforts, not merely expressing agreement. The sons had been trained to understand their father's position and moved together in the same mind. Others seeking justice and judgment followed with wives, children and cattle as affliction increased.

The situation required readiness to leave quickly after the confrontation with the king's authority. The revolution began with a family and then gathered others who chose the law over the security of their former homes.

News reached the king's servants and the army in Jerusalem that men had broken his commandment and gone into hiding. A great number pursued them and attacked on the Sabbath. Mattathias and the people with him had become a problem for the king's imposed religion.

Mattathias and his friends mourned those who had been killed after refusing to fight on the Sabbath. They recognized that following the same course would allow the enemy to root them out of the earth. Their decree was to fight when attacked on the Sabbath rather than all die as those brethren had died.

The decision required agreement: they would live together or die together, and would defend their lives and laws. This was a considered response to what had happened, not a divided collection of private opinions. The present application is the same mind and commitment in doing the spiritual work, rather than a victim's approach to hardship.

A company of Assideans, mighty men voluntarily devoted to the law, joined them. A company is an organized group, not a loose gathering without order. Others fleeing persecution also joined and strengthened them. Men willing to stand became a place for others to gather, and the joined forces struck sinful men.

The movement grew from Mattathias, his sons and friends into a body able to restore what had been destroyed. Their strength and commitment drew those who would not remain among the sellouts. Leadership that actually stands gives the people somewhere to turn.

precepts.why:
“that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you;” Paul required agreement among the brethren at Corinth. The same principle explains the decree of Mattathias and his friends: they had to be of one mind about how they would stand, rather than have divisions destroy their response.

Unity is expressed in action. In the present feast of dedication, men should share the purpose of getting out to camp and enduring hardness. The history of the decree calls for that common understanding and willingness to work.

sense.text:
“Call to remembrance what acts our fathers did in their time; so shall ye receive great honour and an everlasting name.” Mattathias did not encourage his sons with empty confidence. He brought the acts of the fathers back to mind so they could face what lay ahead with faith. Their zeal and willingness to give their lives for the covenant rested on knowing how God had tried and delivered those before them.

A leader facing greater opposing numbers needs more than a carnal estimate of strength. Mattathias' joy in the Lord and connection to the history gave him the strength to stand. The fathers' instruction had preserved that history in him, and now he passed it to his sons.

Abraham was found faithful in temptation. The temptation concerned whether he would obey God when commanded to offer Isaac. This is the kind of struggle Mattathias put before his people: obey and remain with the covenant under hardship, or yield to the Greeks and lose identity and history. Abraham's willingness to go to the end in obedience set a measure of faith for them to remember.

Joseph kept the commandment through distress and became lord of Egypt. His history included his brothers' hostility after his dreams, being cast into a pit, the false account carried back to Jacob, imprisonment and fleeing the temptation to commit adultery with Potiphar's wife. Those troubles did not prevent God from putting him in position to deliver his people during the famine. Mattathias reminded the men that hardship had already been endured by a forefather for a greater purpose.

Phinees' zeal and fervency obtained the covenant of an everlasting priesthood. This Levite example had particular force for Mattathias and his sons. Their people had left comfortable homes and were living in the mountains; a leader had to exhort them through that loss and remind them why faithfulness mattered. Mattathias was a man of the people who used the scriptures to sustain them.

precepts.why:
“God did tempt Abraham,” The test was whether Abraham would obey when commanded to offer the son he loved. Isaac is called his only son even though Ishmael had been born: Isaac was the godly son through whom God's purpose was identified. Merely saying that all are Abraham's children overlooks the distinction among Isaac, Ishmael and the other children.

Isaac saw the fire and wood and asked where the lamb was. Abraham answered, “My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering:” There was no lamb before them then, yet Abraham believed God could deliver while remaining willing to obey. He arranged the altar and wood, bound Isaac and reached for the knife. The pressure upon a father in that moment shows the weight of the test.

The angel stopped him at the point of acting, declaring that his fear of God was shown by not withholding his son. Abraham then saw the ram caught in the thicket. Faith continued to the very end before the provision appeared. Mattathias used this history to strengthen men who likewise had to trust God before they could see how deliverance would come. Judith, Ehud and Gideon supplied the same pattern of a trial answered through faithful action and God's help.

“So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.” The people needed the law read distinctly and its sense explained. So too, men had to guide us through the scriptures to understand who we are, what must be done and what lies ahead; those things had not been made clear to us in the Christian church.

On the holy day they were told to eat the fat, drink the sweet and send portions to those who had nothing prepared. Israel's joy included remembering the poor, not forgetting the people who lacked provision. “for the joy of the Lord is your strength.” Mattathias' strength was joined to that joy in the Lord and the history of his people, rather than depending only on the size of his force.

Israel began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab, sacrificing, eating and bowing before their gods. Men went after Moabite women and were drawn into idolatry. The Lord's anger was kindled when Israel joined Baal-peor. This history makes the need to keep the commandments plain; teaching people not to read the Old Testament removes the very record that explains their judgment.

Moses was commanded to bring judgment upon those joined to the idol so that God's fierce anger could turn away. Phinehas, son of Eleazar and grandson of Aaron, rose from the congregation with a javelin. Mattathias knew this example of a Levite responding to open disobedience. Remembering it explains the zeal being commended and the resolve needed when the people have lost the comfort of their homes for the sake of the law.

sense.text: After Mattathias had spoken, a Jew came publicly to sacrifice on the altar at Modin according to the king's command. The act was not hidden away: the whole gathering could see it, immediately after the appeal to remain zealous for the law. It openly contradicted the stand being made against the oppressor.

“he was inflamed with zeal, and his reins trembled,” His anger was according to judgment, and he slew the man upon the altar. Mattathias' response is connected to the history of his Levite kinsman Phinehas. The mind behind the act was formed by that scriptural example, not by ignorance of his people's law and history.

Mattathias also killed the king's commissioner who compelled men to sacrifice and pulled down the altar. The commissioner represented the pressure and promised rewards used to turn the people from God. Mattathias did not leave that machinery of false sacrifice standing.

His Levite charge helps explain the depth of the response. The holy service was his tribe's responsibility. Seeing its corruption and destruction was therefore not a distant political concern; it struck at the work the Lord had committed to his people.

precepts.why:
An Israelite brought a Midianitish woman before Moses and the congregation while the people were weeping at the tabernacle door. Phinehas saw it, rose with the javelin and followed them into the tent. He thrust both through, and the plague upon Israel was stayed.

The public nature of the offence and the Levite's zeal establish the parallel with the man openly approaching the altar before Mattathias. Mattathias' judgment is explained through that earlier history, which he and his family had been taught. The example connects his mind to his forefathers and the serious responsibility of their priestly office.

The generations of Aaron and Moses frame the Levites' charge at Sinai. They were to keep the charge of the congregation, do the service of the tabernacle and care for its instruments. Later that responsibility concerned the sanctuary and its holy things.

“therefore the Levites shall be mine;” God took Levi in place of the firstborn of Israel. The tribe was set apart for a serious office rather than counted like the other tribal armies. Knowing that commission explains why Mattathias was enraged by the desecration and pulled down the false altar. The reaction grew out of his understanding of the work entrusted to Levi.

sense.text: Even as death approached, Mattathias was still instructing his sons to be zealous for the law and give their lives for the covenant. He continued to turn their minds toward the fathers' acts and the honour of remaining faithful. That was a father's preparation for what his sons would have to face after him.

“Ananias, Azarias, and Misael, by believing were saved out of the flame.” The three holy children were another remembered trial. Mattathias could name them because his own fathers had taught him the testament, and his sons could understand the example because he had taught it to them. History preserved in a family became strength for the whole nation.

Present trials include health concerns, loss of work, children leaving the truth and unbelieving spouses. Return to the fathers when facing those pressures. Their trials show that hardship is not new. The present loss of Israelite identity among families adds another difficulty: many relatives do not even recognize the people to whom this history belongs.

Mattathias' readiness to stand began in that trained mind. He led the people into the wilderness and set the revolution in motion, giving Judas and the other sons strength to carry it forward. Faith must be able to remain firm even before deliverance is visible.

precepts.why:
Nebuchadnezzar demanded that Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego worship the golden image when the music sounded, threatening the fiery furnace if they refused. His question challenged whether any God could deliver them from his hand. The three holy children faced death rather than bow.

They answered that God was able to deliver them. Yet their obedience did not depend on a guarantee that they would escape: “But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.” Even without deliverance, they would not abandon their God.

That is the part of their history that could strengthen Mattathias' sons. He was not merely supplying names from the past; he was recalling the willingness to stand and die rather than submit to idolatry. The same settled faith must be built before a man's own trial arrives.

sense.text: Nehemiah asked about the Jews left from the captivity and the condition of Jerusalem. He heard that the remnant was in great affliction and reproach, the wall broken down and the gates burned. Like Mattathias, he cared about the low state of the people and wanted their restoration.

“I sat down and wept, and mourned certain days,” This was a grown man moved to days of mourning, not a momentary tear. Though he held the king's trust as cupbearer and later received resources and letters for rebuilding, his concern began with the people's distress. Position did not make him indifferent to their condition.

That concern must move men to work rather than choose a victim's posture. The call is for more camps, more cities and more countries reached with the good news of Israel's identity and the commandments. Care for parents and the nation should produce readiness to serve. Men need to care for their health and bodies, keep their eyes on the whole mission like Gideon's three hundred, and motivate the people as Mattathias did.
